newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina raises reward for information on bombings.
newsitem.headline: Argentina raises reward for information on bombings.

text.p: Argentina on Tuesday raised to $3 million the reward it is offering for information on two bomb attacks on its large Jewish community in 1992 and 1994, which killed a total of 115 people.

Interior Minister Carlos Corach announced a $1 million, or 50 percent, raise in the Protection Fund Against International Terrorism to pay a "reward for whoever helps clear up the terrorist attacks against the Israeli Embassy and the AMIA."

A car-bomb attack on the AMIA Jewish community centre in Buenos Aires in July 1994 killed 86 people, injured hundreds more and reduced the building to rubble. Two years earlier, a bomb blast at the embassy killed 29 people.
Argentine police have been criticised by the Jewish community, one of the largest in the world, by Israel and by the United States for their slow progress in investigations into both attacks.

No arrests have been made for the 1992 bombing. A dealer in stolen cars and four policemen have been indicted for allegedly providing the vehicle used in the 1994 attack, but the bombers themselves have not been found.
The blasts have been blamed on the Iranian-backed militant Moslem fundamentalist group Hizbollah.

Corach said police had arrested four men suspected of vandalising Argentina's largest Jewish cemetery, La Tablada, near Buenos Aires, last month. About 100 graves were smashed and daubed with red swastikas and anti-Jewish graffiti.

He told reporters police had "found paint on them which was the same as that used to paint the gravestones in La Tablada." The men have been linked to threats against Jewish hospitals in Buenos Aires.

The vandalism sparked a diplomatic controversy when Argentina reprimanded Israeli Ambassador Yitzhak Aviran for saying: "There are degrees of tolerance beyond which, when the culprits are not found, political stability is affected."
